paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Some musicians take up music because of the excitement inherent in performance. In time, these musicians often find that their initial attraction to the rewards of performance becomes less important as a love for the music itself grows. Others are attracted to the music first and a love of performance may come later. However, while music study and performance are inextricably linked, a performance is usually regarded as a distinct and separate goal, and a unique event, containing a certain amount of unpredictability.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Performance offers the possibility of an intensely satisfying experience. Yet, although complete fulfilment seems within a performer's grasp, it is never promised unconditionally and never fully realized. Notwithstanding these frustrations, musicians and other performers continue to be drawn to performance as the consummation of their achievement. Moreover, as the performance is completed, regardless of its degree of success, they experience the drive to perform again and again, trying each time to make the performance better, more precise, more deeply expressive. Thus they live with the frustration of never quite reaching the faultless outcome they would like to see, but they are never free of their desire to pursue this goal.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: It is helpful for musicians to step back from the intensity of their pursuit. They should look around and realize many of the processes and challenges they face in dealing with musical performance apply to a wide variety of activities. To musicians, performance takes place on a stage, before an audience, or in front of a camera or a microphone. But in reality, performances go on all around us; a large number of routine undertakings can be treated as performance challenges. Adopting such an attitude opens the door to improving skills that contribute significantly not only toward successful musical performance, but also toward achieving many of our other life goals. These endeavours include participation in sports and games, presentations at university or work, social events like weddings, or simply occasions like meeting authority figures or making small talk with the boss.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Under certain external conditions, everyday practicing can begin to take on a more specifically performance-oriented feel for musicians. For example, if they perceive that music-making will result in far-reaching, important consequences, playing or singing tends to go from being simply an enjoyable pastime to being a performance activity. Similarly, if the music they are learning must be ready within a given period, playing or singing that music begins to be regarded as performance oriented. This is especially true if there is a fixed date for this act to take place. Moreover, if they believe they are attempting to play or sing something generally regarded as difficult or unusual, they start to think of the piece in terms of performance. How clearly all these factors are perceived, as well as the intensity of their influence, fluctuates greatly, often changing from day to day or even hour to hour.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: To complicate matters, it remains difficult to identify exactly what it is that enables someone to turn in a successful performance. After decades of study and research, the components that make up successful performance remain elusive, differing not only from individual to individual but also from circumstance to circumstance. Even after years of experience, veteran performers cannot and do not take for granted the skills necessary to turn in a first-rate performance. After even hundreds of successful performances, most performers still have to deal with tension every time. Furthermore, there often seems little correlation between the amount of nervous tension and the resulting degree of success.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Notwithstanding the problems attending performing, there are various means of strengthening one's ability in this area. Self-exploration, for example, helps build esteem and creativity. Preparation to train and consolidate performance skills is also essential, and psychological exercises can be practiced which go some way to generating the stamina and courage required during performance. Feedback too, whether from friends or colleagues or arising from self-reflection, can be priceless. And just occasionally one finds true inspiration; having done so, the desire is there to repeat the experience. All of these means are available to every individual, but they do not simply happen. They must be practiced and reflected upon regularly over a period of time before they begin to take effect, in the same way that healthy lifestyle choices only work if kept up.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: One cannot guarantee that each and every performance will exhibit the best representation of one's skills or abilities. Musicians often feel flat following a performance, and sometimes find it hard to cope with a critical review in the media. Notwithstanding these inescapable hurdles, their ability to deal with the emotion of performance does gradually grow with experience. Their chances of achieving a personal best during the excitement of performance thus tend to grow too. And finally, they do begin to reach their goals of fame or simply self-satisfaction, as a result of a series of successful performances.
